lesson_title: One Dead Bulb, Fifty Dark Lights
hook_text: You plug in last year's festive lights and nothing happens. Not one bulb. One tiny broken filament is to blame. How?
clip_script: Last year's festive lights come out of the cupboard. Plug them in: nothing. Fifty bulbs, all dark, because of one tiny broken filament. They are wired in series, one after another in a single loop. There is only one path for the current, like a single-lane road with no turn-offs. Every charge must pass through every bulb. Block the road anywhere and traffic stops everywhere. That one path also means the current is the same at every point. Now add bulbs: each one is another speed bump on the same road. More resistance, less current, so every bulb gets dimmer. Add cells instead and you get more push, more current, brighter bulbs. Series has its uses: the switch on your wall and the fuse protecting your kettle are in series, so all the current must pass through them.
visual_style: A whiteboard string of bulbs going dark with one cracked bulb highlighted, then a single-lane loop road with cars and speed bumps, then bulbs dimming as more are added.
pacing: A quick problem, a clear analogy, then crisp rules.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and predict what happens when you add a bulb.
